claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution.
The initial alloy has a uniform elemental distribution and minimal intermetallic content.
Thermal exposure under service-regime conditions causes decomposition of the metastable solid solution.
The transformation proceeds through diffusion-mediated nucleation and growth.
Local compositional fluctuations initiate intermetallic precipitation.
The decomposition products are intermetallic compounds enriched in Mg and possibly other elements.
The Mg-rich intermetallic compounds form and coarsen both at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Annealing temperature and composition can affect the length scale of phase decomposition in high-entropy alloys.
Grain-boundary intermetallic phases disrupt the continuity or coherence of the protective oxide film.
Intermetallic precipitation and oxide-film disruption reduce corrosion resistance.
Intermetallic precipitation and oxide-film disruption reduce high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Annealed samples will have a greater volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallic phases than the rapidly quenched baseline.
Annealed samples will have larger Mg-rich intermetallic phases than the rapidly quenched baseline.
The metastable baseline has robust corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The transformation and associated resistance loss occur only above a critical combination of temperature and exposure time at which diffusion is activated.
Below the critical thermal-exposure conditions, the metastable state may persist.
At extremely high temperatures, complete transformation may produce mechanical degradation.
Failure to observe either increased intermetallic content or the corresponding resistance decline in annealed samples would falsify the proposed mechanism.
